title: Finite Dimensional Normed Spaces and Riesz Lemma

items.title: A chosen algebraic basis identifies a finite-dimensional normed space with a coordinate space
items.strategy: Fix an ordered basis e_1,...,e_n of X and define T:K^n->X by T(a_1,...,a_n)=sum a_j e_j. Unique coordinates make T a linear bijection. The pullback norm v->||Tv|| is a norm on the underlying real space of K^n, so the published finite-dimensional norm-equivalence theorem on R^m, with m=n or 2n according to the scalar field, gives two-sided estimates against a standard coordinate norm and hence boundedness of both T and T^{-1}.

items.title: All norms on a finite-dimensional complex normed space are equivalent
items.strategy: Choose a complex basis and transport the two norms to C^n. Reading C^n as R^{2n} by real and imaginary parts turns both transported norms into real norms on a finite-dimensional real vector space, so the published theorem for R^m gives the comparison constants. Transport the inequalities back to the original space and record that the real case has already been published on R^n.

items.title: Every finite-dimensional normed space is Banach
items.strategy: Transport the given norm along a coordinate-space isomorphism. In the real case completeness is the published theorem for R^n in any norm; in the complex case pass to the underlying real space R^{2n} and use the complex norm-equivalence item. Completeness then transfers back across the bounded linear isomorphism.

items.title: A finite-dimensional normed subspace is closed
items.strategy: A finite-dimensional normed subspace is Banach by the previous corollary, and every complete normed subspace is closed in the ambient normed space.

items.title: A linear map from a finite-dimensional normed space is bounded
items.strategy: Choose a basis of the domain. The image norms of the basis vectors give a coefficient-wise estimate on T(sum a_j e_j), and the coordinate-map theorem compares the coordinate sum norm with the given norm on the domain. This yields a global linear bound and hence boundedness.

items.title: Riesz lemma
items.strategy: Pick y outside the proper closed subspace M and set d=dist(y,M)>0. Choose m in M with ||y-m||<d/(1-alpha), normalize x=(y-m)/||y-m||, and estimate dist(x,M) from below by comparing y-m' with y-m for arbitrary m' in M. No best approximation is assumed.

items.title: A normed space is locally compact if and only if it is finite-dimensional
items.strategy: If X is finite-dimensional, the coordinate-map theorem identifies it with K^n and hence with R^n or R^{2n}, which are locally compact. Conversely, if X has a compact neighborhood of 0 then some scaled unit ball has compact closure and is therefore totally bounded. An infinite-dimensional space would then contain arbitrarily large finite 1/2-separated subsets from Riesz's lemma, which a totally bounded set cannot contain.

items.title: Under dependent choice, Riesz lemma builds an infinite separated sequence in the unit sphere
items.strategy: Starting from one unit vector, apply dependent choice to the relation that sends a finite list to an extension by a unit vector whose distance from the span of the earlier vectors exceeds alpha. The finite spans are closed by the finite-dimensional-subspace corollary, so each step is legal.

items.title: The closed unit ball is compact if and only if the normed space is finite-dimensional
items.strategy: If X is finite-dimensional, transport the unit ball to a closed bounded subset of a coordinate space and apply Heine-Borel. Conversely, assume the closed unit ball is compact. Compactness gives total boundedness, so for alpha<1 a finite alpha-net exists. The finite-dimensional span of that net is closed, and one application of Riesz's lemma produces a unit vector farther than alpha from it, contradicting the net property. This infinite-dimensional direction is kept choice-free.

items.title: In an infinite-dimensional normed space the closed unit ball is not compact
items.strategy: Apply the closed-unit-ball characterization contrapositively.

items.title: On an infinite-dimensional normed space, the identity operator is not compact
items.strategy: The identity sends the closed unit ball to itself. Since that ball is not compact in infinite dimension, the identity fails the compact-operator criterion that the unit-ball image be relatively compact.

items.title: A Banach space has no countably infinite Hamel basis
items.strategy: If b_1,b_2,... were a Hamel basis, then the rational span of that sequence would be a countable dense subset. Use the separable complete-metric Baire argument with this fixed dense set to show that a Banach space cannot be a countable union of closed proper finite-dimensional subspaces. Since the partial spans of the basis are closed and exhaust the space, a contradiction follows. The notes record Howard-Tachtsis's sharper choice-strength ledger and why the unrestricted complete-metric Baire theorem would overstate the cost.

items.title: Why the unrestricted complete-metric Baire theorem would overstate the choice cost here
The based Kuratowski distance map into bounded continuous functions
The based Kuratowski distance map is an isometric embedding
items.strategy: For K_o(x)=d(x,.)-d(o,.), the triangle inequality gives ||K_o(x)-K_o(y)||_infty<=d(x,y). Evaluating at z=y and at z=x gives the reverse inequality, so equality holds. The subtraction by d(o,.) is the step that keeps the target bounded when the metric space itself is unbounded.

items.title: Kuratowski-Wojdyslawski embedding theorem
items.strategy: For a bounded metric d, the previous theorem embeds X isometrically into the Banach space C_b(X). Wojdyslawski's argument proves that the image is closed relative to its algebraic convex hull, not in the whole Banach space and not merely in the closed convex hull. For an arbitrary metrizable space, replace d by the canonical bounded equivalent metric d/(1+d): the bounded remetrisation preserves the topology, so the same construction gives a homeomorphic closed embedding into a convex subset of a Banach space.

title: Finite Dimensional Normed Spaces and Riesz Lemma — Examples

items.title: Explicit comparison constants for the standard norms on K^n
items.strategy: Work out the sharp or near-sharp inequalities among the max, Euclidean, and sum norms in low dimensions and compare them with the abstract equivalence theorem.

items.title: An infinite separated subset of the unit sphere
items.strategy: Instantiate the dependent-choice separated-sequence lemma at a concrete alpha, and spell out the first few recursive span-avoidance steps so the abstract construction has a visible witness.

items.title: Heine-Borel fails in ell^2
items.strategy: Use the standard unit vectors in ell^2. They all lie in the closed unit ball, stay sqrt(2) apart, and therefore admit no convergent subsequence. So the closed bounded unit ball is not compact even though the space is Banach.

items.title: The polynomial space admits no complete norm
items.strategy: Show that 1,x,x^2,... is a countably infinite Hamel basis of the polynomial space over the chosen scalar field, then invoke the Banach-space theorem ruling out countably infinite Hamel bases.

items.title: The Kuratowski embedding of a finite metric space
items.strategy: Choose a basepoint, write down the finitely many coordinate functions d(x,.)-d(o,.), and compute the sup distances directly to verify the isometry on a concrete finite metric space.

items.title: Discontinuous linear functionals on Banach spaces are not available in ZF + DC
A choice-free discontinuous linear functional on c_00
items.strategy: Define f(x)=sum n x_n on finitely supported sequences. Finite support makes the sum well defined and linear without any choice principle, while f(e_n)=n and ||e_n||_infty=1 show that the functional is unbounded.
